title: No. 6 — Concerning Dangers from Dissensions Between the States (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The last three numbers of this series were given to listing the dangers we should face, in a state of disunion, from the arms and arts of foreign nations. I shall now go on to describe dangers of a different and perhaps still more alarming kind. These are the dangers that will in all probability flow from dissensions between the States themselves, and from domestic factions and convulsions. They have already been touched on lightly in some places, but they deserve a fuller and more particular investigation.

Only a man far gone in Utopian speculation could seriously doubt that, if these States were wholly disunited, or united only in partial confederacies, the subdivisions into which they might fall would often be at violent odds with one another. To argue that there would be no motives for such contests, and so no contests, would be to forget that men are ambitious, vindictive, and rapacious. To expect harmony to continue among a number of independent, unconnected sovereignties in the same neighborhood would be to ignore the uniform course of human events and to defy the accumulated experience of ages.

The causes of hostility among nations are innumerable. Some operate generally, and almost constantly, on whole societies. These are the love of power, or the desire for pre-eminence and dominion, and the jealousy of power, or the desire for equality and safety. Others have a narrower but equally active influence within their own spheres. Such are the rivalries and competitions of commerce between commercial nations. And there are others, no less numerous than the first two kinds, that arise entirely from private passions: the attachments, enmities, interests, hopes, and fears of leading individuals in the communities to which they belong. Men of this class, whether favorites of a king or of a people, have in too many instances abused the confidence placed in them. Under the pretext of some public motive, they have not hesitated to sacrifice the national tranquillity to personal advantage or personal gratification.

The celebrated Pericles, to satisfy the resentment of a prostitute,(1) attacked, defeated, and destroyed the city of the SAMMIANS, at the cost of much of the blood and treasure of his countrymen. The same man was the original author of that famous and fatal war that the Grecian annals call the PELOPONNESIAN war. Perhaps he was driven by private spite against the MEGARENSIANS,(2) another nation of Greece. Perhaps he wanted to avoid a prosecution that threatened him as an accomplice in the supposed theft of the sculptor Phidias.(3) Perhaps he wanted to be rid of the accusations being prepared against him for squandering the funds of the state to buy popularity.(4) Or perhaps it was a combination of all these causes. After various turns of fortune, interruptions, and renewals, that war ended in the ruin of the Athenian commonwealth.

The ambitious cardinal who was prime minister to Henry VIII let his vanity aspire to the triple crown.(5) He hoped to win that splendid prize through the influence of the Emperor Charles V. To secure the favor and support of this enterprising and powerful monarch, he pushed England into a war with France. This went against the plainest dictates of policy and risked the safety and independence of the kingdom he guided by his counsels, and of Europe in general. For if there ever was a sovereign who seemed likely to realize the project of universal monarchy, it was the Emperor Charles V, and Wolsey was both the instrument and the dupe of his intrigues.

The influence that the bigotry of one woman,(6) the petulance of another,(7) and the cabals of a third(8) had on the policy, the ferments, and the pacifications of a considerable part of Europe in their time has been discussed too often not to be generally known.

It would be an unnecessary waste of time to multiply examples of the part that personal considerations play in producing great national events, foreign or domestic, according to the direction they take. Those with only a superficial acquaintance with the sources of such examples will recall a variety of them for themselves. Those with a tolerable knowledge of human nature do not need such lights to form their own opinion of how real and how far-reaching that influence is. Perhaps, however, a reference to a case that has recently happened among ourselves may properly be made to illustrate the general principle. If Shays had not been a DESPERATE DEBTOR, it is much to be doubted whether Massachusetts would have been plunged into a civil war.

But despite the agreeing testimony of experience on this point, there are still visionary or designing men who stand ready to defend the paradox of perpetual peace between the States, though they be broken apart and estranged from one another. The character of republics, they say, is peaceful. The spirit of commerce, they say, tends to soften the manners of men and to extinguish those inflammable humors that have so often burst into war. Commercial republics like ours, they say, will never be inclined to exhaust themselves in ruinous contests with each other. They will be governed by mutual interest and will cultivate a spirit of mutual friendship and harmony.

We may ask these projectors in politics: is it not the true interest of all nations to cultivate the same benevolent and philosophic spirit? If it is, have they in fact pursued it? Has it not, on the contrary, always been found that momentary passions and immediate interest control human conduct more actively and more imperiously than general or remote considerations of policy, utility, or justice? Have republics in practice been less addicted to war than monarchies? Are not the former run by MEN as well as the latter? Do not aversions, preferences, rivalries, and desires for unjust gains affect nations as well as kings? Are not popular assemblies often subject to impulses of rage, resentment, jealousy, greed, and other irregular and violent tendencies? Is it not well known that their decisions are often governed by a few individuals in whom they place confidence, and so are likely to be colored by the passions and views of those individuals? Has commerce so far done anything more than change the objects of war? Is the love of wealth any less domineering and enterprising a passion than the love of power or glory? Since commerce became the prevailing system of nations, have there not been as many wars founded on commercial motives as were once caused by greed for territory or dominion? Has not the spirit of commerce, in many instances, supplied new incentives to the appetite for both? Let experience, the least fallible guide of human opinions, be appealed to for the answer.

Sparta, Athens, Rome, and Carthage were all republics, and two of them, Athens and Carthage, were of the commercial kind. Yet they fought wars, offensive and defensive, as often as the neighboring monarchies of their times. Sparta was little better than a well-regulated camp, and Rome never had enough of carnage and conquest.

Carthage was a commercial republic, yet she was the aggressor in the very war that ended in her destruction. Hannibal had carried her arms into the heart of Italy and to the gates of Rome. Only then did Scipio defeat him in the territories of Carthage, and in turn conquer the commonwealth.

Venice, in later times, took part more than once in wars of ambition. Finally she became an object of concern to the other Italian states, and Pope Julius II managed to form against her that formidable league,(9) which dealt a deadly blow to the power and pride of this haughty republic.

The provinces of Holland took a leading and conspicuous part in the wars of Europe until they were overwhelmed by debts and taxes. They fought furious contests with England for dominion of the sea, and they were among the most persevering and implacable opponents of Louis XIV.

In the government of Britain, the representatives of the people make up one branch of the national legislature. Commerce has been the predominant pursuit of that country for ages. Few nations, nevertheless, have gone to war more often, and in numerous instances the wars of that kingdom have come from the people.

There have been, if I may put it so, almost as many popular wars as royal wars. On various occasions the cries of the nation and the importunities of their representatives have dragged their monarchs into war, or kept them in it, against their inclinations and sometimes against the real interests of the State. Consider the memorable struggle for superiority between the rival houses of AUSTRIA and BOURBON, which kept Europe in a flame for so long. It is well known that the English antipathy against the French, backing the ambition, or rather the greed, of a favorite leader,(10) prolonged that war beyond the limits set by sound policy and, for a considerable time, against the views of the court.

The wars of these last two nations have in great measure grown out of commercial considerations: the desire to supplant, and the fear of being supplanted, whether in particular branches of trade or in the general advantages of trade and navigation. Sometimes there was also the more blameworthy desire to share in the commerce of other nations without their consent.

The last war but one between Britain and Spain sprang from the attempts of British merchants to carry on an illicit trade with the Spanish Main. These unjustifiable practices on their side produced severity on the Spanish side toward British subjects, and that severity was no more justifiable, because it went beyond the bounds of just retaliation and could be charged with inhumanity and cruelty. Many of the English taken on the Spanish coast were sent to dig in the mines of Potosi. By the usual progress of a spirit of resentment, the innocent were soon confounded with the guilty in indiscriminate punishment. The complaints of the merchants kindled a violent flame throughout the nation. It soon broke out in the House of Commons and was passed from that body to the ministry. Letters of reprisal were granted, and war followed. Its consequences overthrew all the alliances that had been formed only twenty years before, with sanguine expectations of the most beneficial fruits.

This summary shows what has happened in other countries whose situations most resembled our own. What reason can we have, after it, to trust those reveries that would lead us to expect peace and cordiality among the members of the present confederacy once they are separated? Have we not already seen enough of the fallacy and extravagance of those idle theories that have amused us with promises of an exemption from the imperfections, weaknesses, and evils that attend society in every form? Is it not time to wake from the deceitful dream of a golden age, and to adopt as a practical maxim for guiding our political conduct that we, like the other inhabitants of the globe, are still far from the happy empire of perfect wisdom and perfect virtue?

Let the extreme depression to which our national dignity and credit have sunk speak. Let the problems felt everywhere from a lax and ill-managed administration of government speak. Let the revolt of a part of the State of North Carolina, the recent menacing disturbances in Pennsylvania, and the actual insurrections and rebellions in Massachusetts speak—!

The general sense of mankind is so far from agreeing with the tenets of those who try to lull our apprehensions of discord and hostility between the States, in the event of disunion, that long observation of the progress of society has made it a sort of axiom in politics that nearness of situation makes nations natural enemies. An intelligent writer says on this subject, to this effect: "NEIGHBORING NATIONS (says he) are naturally enemies of each other unless their common weakness forces them to league in a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC, and their constitution prevents the differences that neighborhood occasions, extinguishing that secret jealousy which disposes all states to aggrandize themselves at the expense of their neighbors."(11) This passage points out the EVIL and at the same time suggests the REMEDY.
